title: Drink Water from Your Own Cistern
summary: The father warns his son that the forbidden woman's words are sweet as honey at first but bitter as wormwood in the end, leading down to death. Going to her costs a man his strength, his years, and his wealth, and leaves him at life's end groaning with regret. Instead, the son should find joy and delight in his own wife, knowing that the LORD sees every path and that a man's own sins become the cords that trap him.
story: Chapter 2 briefly introduced the forbidden woman as one of two dangers wisdom guards against. Chapters 5 to 7 return to her at length, making sexual faithfulness the most developed practical topic of the book's opening section. Chapter 5 is the first of these three warnings. It is also, unusually, a celebration: alongside the warning it offers a frank and joyful picture of married love. The chapter fits the wider biblical story in which marriage, instituted at creation (Genesis 2:24), is a covenant bond that the seventh commandment protects (Exodus 20:14).
historical:
No historical event stands behind the chapter, and its date is tied to the uncertain date of chapters 1 to 9 as a whole. Its concerns are those of any settled society in the ancient Near East, where adultery threatened not only personal relationships but inheritance, property, and the stability of households and clans. Israel's law treated adultery as a capital crime (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22), though Proverbs never mentions the death penalty. Instead it focuses on the natural consequences: public shame before the assembly (verse 14), the loss of wealth and labor to strangers (verse 10), and a wasted life.

The mention of the whole assembly in verse 14 probably refers to the community gathered to judge or to hear a public matter, as happened at the city gate. A man exposed in adultery lost standing before his whole town.
cultural:
Water was precious in the land of Israel, which depended on seasonal rains. Households carved cisterns into rock to catch and store rainwater, and a family's own well or cistern was valuable private property. Letting your springs flow into the streets (verse 16) would be pure waste. The father uses this image to speak with restraint about sexual love: a man should find his satisfaction within his own marriage, not scatter it abroad. Similar imagery appears in the Song of Songs, where the bride is called a spring enclosed and a garden fountain (Song of Songs 4:12-15).

Wormwood (verse 4) is a bitter plant, used in the Bible as a picture of the bitterness of sin and judgment. A double-edged sword was the sharpest weapon a soldier carried. A doe and a fawn (verse 19) were admired in ancient love poetry for their grace and beauty. The phrase wife of your youth reflects a culture of early marriage, in which a man's first wife was the companion of his whole adult life.
literary: The chapter has four movements. Verses 1 to 6 describe the woman: sweet lips, bitter end, feet going down to death. Verses 7 to 14 describe the cost of going to her, closing with the man's own regretful speech at the end of life, a dramatic device that lets the son hear his future self. Verses 15 to 20 turn from warning to invitation, using extended water imagery and ending in a question: why be captivated by a stranger? Verses 21 to 23 conclude with theology: God sees, sin traps, and folly leads astray. The verb shagah, to be captivated or intoxicated, appears in verses 19 and 20 and then, with a sharp turn, in verse 23, where the fool is led astray. The man will be intoxicated by something: his wife's love, or his own folly.

outline.t: The cost of going to her door
Rejoice in the wife of your youth

doctrines.note: Marriage is presented as the right place for sexual love and joy, not merely as a restraint. The command to rejoice in the wife of your youth treats married delight as good and worth guarding.
Verse 22 says the wicked man's iniquities entrap him and the cords of his sin hold him fast. Sin is not only a broken rule but a trap that tightens around the one who commits it.
Verse 21 grounds the whole warning in God's knowledge: a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD. No secret sin is hidden from him, and he weighs every path.

words.note: Zur, to be a stranger. The participle, zarah, is used for the forbidden woman in verses 3 and 20, and the related word appears in verses 10 and 17 for strangers who take a man's wealth. The word marks someone outside the proper circle, here outside one's own marriage covenant, whatever her nationality.

Shagah, to stray, reel, or be intoxicated. It can describe a drunk man staggering or a sheep wandering. Verse 19 uses it positively: be captivated by your wife's love. Verse 20 asks why be captivated by another, and verse 23 uses it of the fool led astray. The repetition makes the choice clear.

Musar, discipline or instruction. It means correction that forms a person, whether by teaching or by painful consequence. In verse 12 the ruined man confesses that he hated discipline, and in verse 23 he dies for lack of it. The book's opening line named musar as one of its purposes (1:2).

christ: Jesus deepened the teaching of this chapter when he said that looking at a woman with lustful intent is already adultery in the heart (Matthew 5:27-28), locating faithfulness where Proverbs 4:23 located the springs of life. Paul uses marriage as a picture of Christ's love for the church, calling husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25-32). The faithfulness Proverbs asks of a husband reflects the covenant faithfulness of God, who, in the prophets, is the husband of his people even when they are unfaithful (Hosea 2-3), and which Christ fulfills as the bridegroom. And for those who have already walked the path this chapter warns against, the New Testament proclaims forgiveness and cleansing in Christ (1 Corinthians 6:9-11).

hard.q: Doesn't this chapter blame the woman and speak only to men?
hard.a: The chapter is addressed to a son, because the book's opening section is written as a father's instruction to a young man, and it describes the temptation he will face. That is its frame, not a claim that men are innocent and women guilty. In fact the chapter places the weight of responsibility on the young man: he is the one who must keep his path far from her door, and verses 21 to 23 say that his own iniquities trap him. Elsewhere, Proverbs speaks equally hard words about men who are violent, deceitful, or sexually predatory, and it praises wise women, above all in chapter 31. Many readers apply the chapter's warning in both directions, since the dynamics it describes (sweet words, hidden costs, wasted years, public ruin) apply to anyone tempted to betray a marriage. The chapter's goal is not to demonize women but to protect marriages and households.

questions: The chapter pictures a man at the end of his life regretting that he hated discipline. What do you hope to be able to say, looking back?
Why do you think the father pairs his warning with such a warm picture of married love, rather than warning alone?
Verse 22 describes sin as cords that entangle. Have you seen a choice that looked small become a trap?
